belief: Taking medication means I'm not really myself.
origins: Some medicines change mood, energy, or thinking. Some people feel flattened or foggy, and others worry that treatment changes their personality or covers their “real” feelings. Fear of losing oneself makes people stop treatment on their own.
teaches: God knows who you are: “O LORD, You have searched me and known me” (Psalm 139:1). Your identity is not a chemical state. It is rooted in being made by God and belonging to Him. Paul says, “Though our outer self is wasting away, yet our inner self is being renewed day by day.” Treatment that helps your brain or body function better can free the real you, not erase you. If you feel different in a worrying way, tell your doctor. Do not stop on your own.
self_statements: I am not me on this medicine.
It is changing who I am.
I would rather feel pain than lose myself.
errors: Believing I am either fully myself or altered.
Predicting that I will lose my identity.
Feeling different and concluding that I am not myself.
questions: What exactly feels different, and when did it start?
Was I more myself before, or was I in pain or fog?
What do family and friends notice?
What do I want my doctor to know?
What helps me feel like me?
What does it mean that God knows my true self?
truth: God knows me completely, and my identity does not rest on how I feel at the moment. If treatment is dulling me, my doctor can adjust it. I can seek the real me with care and honesty.
hw_truths: My inner self is being renewed.
I can tell my doctor what I feel.
log: Each week, note one thing that felt like you.
actions: Report side effects or changes honestly.
Make changes only with your doctor.
prayer: Lord, You know the real me. Guide my doctors, give me honesty, and help me live as Your child, whatever my treatment. Amen.
